title: Toxic Co-workers: How to Handle Difficult People

overview.title: Toxic Co-workers: How to Handle Difficult People
overview.goal: Describe difficult workplace behaviour, use six expressions, discuss strategies and advise a colleague using gerunds and infinitives.

vocabulary: speak while another person is talking
say that another person's work is yours
control every small detail of someone's work
say clearly what behaviour you will accept
share unverified stories about other people
say what you think when something is unfair

steps.title: Lesson information
steps.instruction: Look at the lesson goals. What do you already know about difficult workplace relationships?
source: B1 · Adults · 50 minutes
Goal: describe difficult co-worker behaviour and suggest respectful ways to respond.
Vocabulary: interrupt someone; take credit for someone's work; micromanage; set boundaries; spread rumours; speak up.
Grammar: gerunds and infinitives after common verbs (avoid doing, decide to do, suggest doing, agree to do).
Reading: practical advice about dealing with a difficult team member.
Speaking: describe a work situation, choose a response and practise a constructive conversation.
steps.teacherNotes: 3 min. Present outcomes without pre-teaching solutions. Ask: Does disagreeing with a colleague always mean they are toxic? Focus on observable actions, not labelling people.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.instruction: Look at these everyday office situations. Which behaviour is the hardest to deal with? Explain your reasons.

cards: A colleague keeps speaking over others in meetings.
Someone presents your idea as their own.
A teammate checks every little step you take.

source: Discuss: Which situation have you seen before, even outside work? How did people respond?
Is it better to talk to the person immediately, wait, or ask a manager? Does the answer depend on the situation?
Mini-task: Give one example of an annoying habit that is NOT necessarily toxic.
items: Which situation is an example of taking credit for someone else's work?
A colleague asks for an update.
A colleague says your idea was theirs.
Taking credit means claiming somebody else's achievement.
What is usually a sensible first step in a minor conflict?
Focus on the behaviour and its effect.
Which sentence gives an observation rather than a personal insult?
I was interrupted twice in the meeting.
An observation is easier to discuss constructively.
steps.teacherNotes: 6 min. Prioritise 4 minutes of speaking; use choices as a quick check, not the main activity.

steps.title: Topical vocabulary
steps.instruction: Match the six expressions to their meanings, then make one short example about a team.
source: interrupt someone · take credit for someone's work · micromanage · set boundaries · spread rumours · speak up
After matching, choose TWO expressions and say: 'A difficult co-worker might...' or 'A good manager should...'.
items: stop somebody while they are speaking
say something when there is a problem
steps.teacherNotes: 7 min. Exactly six active phrases. After checking, demand productive examples; avoid introducing extra target phrases.

steps.title: Vocabulary in action
steps.instruction: Complete the six sentences with expressions from the previous section. Then tell your teacher which sentence sounds most realistic.
source: Use each target expression once. Some verbs may need a different form.
Model: 'I prefer to speak up when I notice something unfair.'
items: Our new colleague often ___ when I am explaining my ideas.
I spent two days preparing the slides, but Tom tried to ___.
My manager likes to ___ every small task instead of trusting us.
It is important to ___ if people keep contacting you late at night.
Some people ___ about colleagues they hardly know.
If you see something unfair, it can help to ___ politely.
steps.teacherNotes: 5 min. Recycle only the six active expressions. Ask for reasons, not just answers.

steps.title: Reading: A difficult team member
steps.instruction: Read the case study. Decide whether the manager's response was fair, then answer the questions.
source: A few months ago, Maya joined a small marketing team. She enjoyed the work, but meetings soon became stressful. One colleague, Daniel, often interrupted her and took credit for ideas she had shared earlier. He also checked every detail of her projects, even though he was not her manager.

At first, Maya avoided saying anything because she wanted to be friendly. But the situation got worse. During a meeting, Daniel presented Maya's campaign idea as his own. She felt embarrassed, yet she did not want to start an argument in front of everyone.

Maya decided to keep notes about specific incidents. She then asked Daniel to have a private conversation. Instead of calling him 'toxic', she explained what had happened: 'When you present my ideas without mentioning me, I feel that my work is not recognised.' She suggested agreeing on who would present each part of the next project.

Daniel seemed surprised. He apologised for not giving her credit, although he did not agree with everything she said. They made a clearer plan for future meetings. Maya also spoke to their manager, who encouraged the whole team to share responsibilities more openly.

The problem did not disappear overnight, but Maya learned that setting boundaries and speaking up calmly could improve the situation. Her main lesson was simple: describe actions, explain their effect, and ask for a specific change.
items: Why did Maya avoid speaking to Daniel at first?
She wanted to keep relationships friendly.
How did Maya begin her conversation?
She described an action and its effect.
She demanded that he be fired.
What is the key message of the text?
Discuss specific behaviour and propose a change.
Every problem needs an immediate formal complaint.
steps.teacherNotes: 8 min: first read for the main idea, then details. Follow-up: Was Maya right to speak to a manager as well? Accept reasoned alternatives.

steps.title: Grammar: Gerunds and infinitives
steps.instruction: Notice the verb pattern, choose the correct form, then make two more sentences about workplace communication.
source: Some verbs are followed by -ing: avoid arguing, suggest talking, keep interrupting, practise listening.
Other verbs are followed by to + verb: decide to speak, agree to listen, want to help, need to change.
Compare: 'She stopped interrupting' (she no longer did it) and 'She stopped to speak' (she paused another activity in order to speak).
Your task: explain which pattern is used after avoid, suggest, decide and agree.
items: It's best to avoid ___ colleagues in public.
Please stop ___ me when I'm presenting.
I want ___ boundaries without being rude.
steps.teacherNotes: 7 min. Ellicit -ing vs to-infinitive; distinguish stop doing vs stop to do. Ask for 2 original examples.

steps.title: Practice: Choose a response
steps.instruction: You are in an uncomfortable work situation. Choose a response, explain why, and improve it in your own words.

cards: You are interrupted for the third time.
A colleague expects instant replies after work.
Someone takes credit for the team's idea.

source: Role-play 1: 'I haven't finished explaining my point. Could I just finish?'
Role-play 2: Use a polite boundary: 'I can reply tomorrow morning. Is that OK?'
Role-play 3: Suggest a concrete next step: 'Let's agree on who presents which part.'
items: Which response helps if somebody interrupts you?
Could I finish my point, please?
I will spread rumours about you.
Which sentence sets a clear boundary?
I can answer work messages during office hours.
I will never speak to you again.
What is a constructive way to respond to stolen credit?
Could we mention everyone's contributions in the presentation?
steps.teacherNotes: 6 min: use choices only as a launchpad for role-play. Change roles and ask learner to produce 2–3 complete lines.

steps.title: Let's talk: Solve the problem
steps.instruction: Final task: advise a friend whose colleague keeps interrupting them, takes credit and sends messages late at night.
source: Round 1 (2 min): Describe the problem using at least THREE expressions from today's vocabulary.
Round 2 (3 min): Role-play a calm conversation. Use at least TWO gerunds and TWO infinitives (e.g., 'I suggest talking...' and 'I decided to...').
Round 3 (2 min): Your partner disagrees. Respond politely, set one boundary and agree on a next step.
Reflection (1 min): Which phrase would be most useful in your real life? What will you do differently?
steps.teacherNotes: 8 min. Performance criteria: (1) three target phrases used accurately, (2) at least one correct -ing and one correct to-infinitive, (3) a respectful request and specific next step, (4) clear and understandable speech. Give one correction and one repeat opportunity. Homework remains the previously assigned independent task, unchanged.
